'''''Elatine hexandra''''', the '''six-stamened waterwort''', is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Elatinaceae]], which grows in shallow water around lakes and pools in Europe from Ireland to Romania. It is declining due to drainage and water pollution and is therefore protected in several countries.

==Description==
[[File:Elatine hexandra sl22.jpg|thumb|left|Detail of the flower]]
Six-stamened waterwort is a small annual to short-lived perennial herb with creeping stems up to about 8 cm long, which root at the nodes. It is entirely glabrous, with opposite pairs of elliptical to spathulate leaves about 7 mm long, which are borne on short petioles. At the tip of each leaf is a tiny, black [[hydathode]]. There are also minute stipules at the base of the leaf stalks. The stems and leaves are usually yellowy-green under water, becoming bright green or reddish when exposed on bare mud.

The flowers are usually solitary or sometimes in short [[Cyme (botany)|cyme]]s arising at the leaf nodes. Each flower has three (sometimes 4) sepals and the same number of pinkish-white petals. There are six [[stamen]]s and 3-5 [[Style (botany)|styles]]. The flower stalks (pedicels) elongate as the fruit matures, bearing a capsule with four valves. The seeds are cylindrical, brownish, up to about 0.7 mm long and slightly curved.<ref name=Sell1>{{cite book |last1=Sell |first1=Peter |last2=Murrell |first2=Gina |title=Flora of Great Britain and Ireland, vol. 1 |date=2018 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge|isbn=978-0-521-55335-3}}</ref><ref name=Schou>{{Cite book |last1=Schou |first1=J.C. |last2=Moeslund |first2=B. |last3=van de Weyer |first3=K. |last4=Lansdown |first4=R.V. |last5=Wiegleb |first5=G. |last6=Holm |first6=P. |last7=Baastrup-Spohr |first7=L. |last8=Sand-Jensen |first8=K. |display-authors=1 |title=Aquatic Plants of Northern and Central Europe including Britain and Ireland |publisher=Princeton University Press |year=2023 |isbn=978-0-691-25101-1 |location=Princeton, N.J.}}</ref>
[[File:Elatine hexandra sl40.jpg|thumb|The seeds are cylindrical and slightly curved]]

==Identification==
In Britain and Northern Europe it is most likely to be confused with ''[[Elatine hydropiper]]'', but that species has no (or very short) pedicels and strongly curved (horseshoe-shaped) fruit. The numbers of the flower parts is less reliable, as ''E. hexandra'' does occasionally have 4 sepals, 4 petals and 8 stamens (rather than 3, 3 and 6), as does ''E. hydropiper''.<ref name=Stace>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |location=Suffolk |publisher=C&M Floristics |edition=4th |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Popiela |first=Agnieszka |last2=Łysko |first2=Andrzej |title=The distribution of species of the section ''Elatinella'' Seub. (''Elatine'' L., Elatinaceae) in Europe |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/263007502_The_distribution_of_species_of_the_section_Elatinella_Seub_Elatine_L_Elatinaceae_in_Europe |journal=Festschrift Profesora, Kraków, Ogród Botaniczny – Instytut Botaniki UJ: 147–xx. |pages=147}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
The scientific name ''Elatine hexandra'' was published by [[Augustin Pyramus de Candolle|de Candolle]] and [[Jean-Baptiste Lamarck|Lamarck]] in their work ''Flore Française'' ([https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/50110823#page/625/mode/1up 3rd edition, vol. 5, p. 609]) in 1805.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Elatine hexandra {{!}} International Plant Names Index |url=https://www.ipni.org/n/324687-1 |access-date=2024-11-26 |website=www.ipni.org}}</ref> Jean Marie Lapierre (1754-1834), in 1802, had named it ''Tillaea hexandra'' but de Candolle realised that this was the wrong genus (''Tillaea'' is now included in ''[[Crassula]]'').

It has no recognised subspecies and it is not known to hybridise with any other plants.<ref name=hybrids>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |last2=Preston |first2=C.D. |last3=Pearman |first3=D.A. |title=Hybrid Flora of the British Isles |date=2015 |publisher=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |location=Bristol}}</ref>

The scientific name is derived from the [[Ancient Greek]] word for a [[Abies alba|silver fir]], Ἐλάτη (Elátē), which also means an [[oar]], as ship parts were usually made of this light, strong wood. It probably alludes to the shape of the leaves.<ref name=Leighton>{{cite book |last1=Leighton |first1=W.A. |title=A Flora of Shropshire |date=1841 |publisher=John van Voorst |location=London}}</ref> The specific epithet ''hexandra'' is simply Greek for "six stamens".

==Distribution and status==
The range of six-stamened waterwort extends throughout Europe, possibly just into North Africa and westwards to the Azores. The eastward limit is in Poland and Romania.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Elatine hexandra (Lapierre) DC. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/5646074 |access-date=2024-11-26 |website=www.gbif.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Elatine hexandra (Lapierre) DC. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:324687-1 |access-date=2024-11-26 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref>

Sites where this species occur are generally lowland, although it has been found as high as 440 m at Lough Ferta in Ireland, and 425 m at Llyn Gynon in Wales.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Pearman |first1=D.A. |title=Altitudinal Limits of British Plants, 2021 |url=https://bsbi.org/altitudes}}</ref> An old record of it at 490 m in Scotland has never been verified.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stewart |first1=A. |last2=Pearman |first2=D.A. |last3=Preston |first3=C.D. |title=Scarce Plants in Britain |date=1994 |publisher=Joint Nature Conservation Committee |location=Peterborough}}</ref>

Its conservation status, globally, is Least Concern,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Six-stamened Waterwort, Elatine hexandra |url=https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/167853/6397822 |access-date=25 November 2024 |website=The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species}}</ref> but there are regions such as [[Picardy]] and [[Île-de-France]], where it is considered to be rare and threatened.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Élatine à six étamines |url=https://inpn.mnhn.fr/espece/cd_nom/95858?lg=fr |access-date=26 November 2024 |website=Inventaire National du Patrimoine Naturel}}</ref>

In all the British counties where it is found, it is considered to be an [[axiophyte]], or plant of conservation importance, owing to its affinity for low-nutrient water bodies.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Axiophytes – Botanical Society of Britain & Ireland |url=https://bsbi.org/axiophytes |access-date=2024-11-26 |language=en-GB}}</ref>

==Habitat and ecology==
[[File:Elatine hexandra sward.jpg|thumb|Habitat of six-stamened waterwort in a sandy pool]]
This is a plant of clear-water lakes and pools, usually with slightly acidic water and low levels of fertility. Its [[Indicator value|Ellenberg values]] in Britain are L=7, F=10, R=5, N=4, and S=0.<ref name="Hill-2004">{{cite web |last1=Hill |first1=M.O. |last2=Preston |first2=C.D. |last3=Roy |first3=D.B. |title=PLANTATT - Attributes of British and Irish Plants - Spreadsheet |url=https://www.brc.ac.uk/biblio/plantatt-attributes-british-and-irish-plants-spreadsheet |publisher=UK Biological Records Centre}}</ref> It has been found at depths up to 3 m in very clear conditions, but is more normally found around in water about 10 cm deep.<ref name="Schou" />

When growing submerged, the flowers are [[Cleistogamy|cleistogamous]], remaining closed up and self-pollinating. When a plant is exposed on bare mud in the summer, however, the flowers open in the normal way and are pollinated by insects. Its fruiting biology was studied by Salisbury in 1964, who found that a typical seed capsule contained about 36 seeds (roughly 12 in each of the 3 sections), but that flowers with 4 carpels could produce as many as 79 seeds. He calculated that a single plant could produce as many as 27,000 seeds if it was growing on exposed mud, but much fewer if self-pollinating under water, which shows how it is adapted to react quickly to favourable conditions in an occasional dry summer. Seed germination rates were also strongly linked to exposure to bright sunlight.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Salisbury |first=J. |title=On the reproduction and biology of ''Elatine hexandra'' (Lapierre) DC. (Elatinaceae); a typical species of exposed mud |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/4108455 |journal=Kew Bulletin |volume=2 |pages=139-147}}</ref> The seeds do not float, but can remain viable under water or buried for many years.<ref name="Schou" />

==Uses==
[[File:Elatine hexandra sl64.jpg|thumb|The leaves are in opposite pairs and somewhat paddle-shaped.]]
This is a useful plant to keep in aquariums, as it is fast-growing but small.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Six-stamened Waterwort |url=http://www.wildflowerweb.co.uk/plant/1987/six-stamened-waterwort |access-date=26 November 2024 |website=Wild Flower Web}}</ref>
